script.opening: (Frustrated, embarrassed; keeps hands out of view at first.) "Doctor, these white patches keep appearing and spreading — my hands, around my eyes and mouth. Against my skin they really show, and people stare, they ask what's wrong with me, some won't shake my hand. My family are worried what people will say. I feel like a freak, honestly. I just want to know what it is, whether it's catching, and can you make it go away?"

facts.text: Started about five months ago on the backs of both hands, then around the eyes and mouth. "They're getting bigger." Completely white, flat, sharp edges. If asked: no itch, pain, scaling or numbness — "They don't feel any different." Will show his hands and face on camera if asked.
No rash or burn beforehand. A few white hairs in his eyebrow. If asked: no tiredness, weight change, palpitations, thirst or passing more urine. Feels well in himself.
Nothing significant. If asked about family: "My aunt in India has thyroid tablets, I think." Nobody in the family has white patches that he knows of. No medicines, no allergies.
Works in a mobile phone shop, customer-facing. Lives with parents and younger sister. Doesn't smoke, drinks occasionally. Has been wearing long sleeves and avoiding handshakes at work.

Only if asked what it is like for him: "I hide my hands. I don't want to meet people. When someone won't shake my hand I just want to disappear." A customer asked if it was catching. His mum has been trying home remedies and worries about "what people will say" — he is meant to be meeting a family friend's daughter with a view to marriage.
If asked: "I'm avoiding people. I feel low, but I'm not going to do anything stupid." Sleeping okay. No thoughts of self-harm.
If asked: the patches burn quickly in the sun; he hasn't been using sun cream.

Guarded and embarrassed at first. Volunteer the patches and the staring; hold back the marriage pressure and low mood unless the doctor asks about the effect on his life. If the doctor only talks about creams, ask "But is it catching? My family need to know." When told clearly it isn't infectious and isn't his fault, relax: "That would help. They'd believe it from a doctor."

ice.ideas: "I was scared it was catching, or something serious inside."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the staring, being refused handshakes, his family's worry about what people will say and a possible marriage introduction. He feels like "a freak" and has started to hide away.
ice.expectations: "To know what it is, that it's not catching — and something to make it go away."

checkpoints.text: Diagnoses VITILIGO confidently (well-demarcated depigmented macules, characteristic sites, spreading) and reassures FIRMLY that it is NOT contagious, NOT dangerous to physical health, and not his or anyone’s fault — correcting the contagion myth
Screens for associated AUTOIMMUNE disease — especially THYROID (TFTs/antibodies) — and is alert to others (pernicious anaemia, T1DM, alopecia areata)

Discusses TREATMENT realistically: topical corticosteroids/calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy and specialist options via dermatology, cosmetic camouflage, and SUN PROTECTION of depigmented skin — with honest expectations (variable, slow, some areas respond poorly), avoiding false promises of a "cure"
Refers to DERMATOLOGY appropriately (for treatment/phototherapy, diagnostic confirmation if needed, rapidly spreading disease) and signposts cosmetic camouflage services

Recognises and addresses the dominant PSYCHOSOCIAL impact: validates the stigma, staring, family/cultural pressure and identity distress, screens mood, and offers psychological support and patient support groups/charities

Acknowledges what the condition MEANS to him — the stigma, the "freak" feeling, the relationship/identity impact — and validates it as the central issue, rather than treating it as a purely dermatological problem
Responds with warmth and without minimising; equips him (and his family) to counter the contagion myth and stigma, restoring some agency

Safety-nets and follows up: thyroid/autoimmune results, dermatology referral and camouflage/sun-protection advice, psychological and peer support, mood review, and follow-up — treating the person and the meaning alongside the skin

worked.txt: "Let me give you the name and the most important fact first: this is vitiligo — the skin loses its colour in patches because the immune system stops the colour-making cells working. The crucial thing, and please tell anyone who needs to hear it: it is absolutely NOT catching. No one can get it from you, shaking your hand is completely safe, and it’s not dangerous to your health. It’s not your fault and nothing you did caused it."

"And I’m not going to pretend this is just a skin thing — because what you’ve described, the staring, people pulling their hand away, feeling like a freak, your family worrying what others will say — THAT is the hardest part, and it’s completely understandable. That matters to me as much as the patches themselves."

"There are a couple of things I’ll check — vitiligo can come along with an underactive or overactive thyroid, so a blood test for that. Otherwise you’re physically well, and this is about the skin and, just as much, about how you’re coping."

"On making it go away — I’ll be honest with you rather than over-promise. There are treatments that can help: creams, and special light treatment through the skin specialists, which can bring some colour back or stop it spreading — but they work slowly and unevenly, and some areas respond better than others. There’s also excellent skin-camouflage make-up that matches your tone really well if you want to cover patches. And the white skin burns easily, so sun protection matters."

"Most importantly — how is this affecting you in yourself? Your confidence, your mood, relationships? … You’re not a freak, and you’re far from alone — it’s common, including in people of South Asian heritage. There are support groups of people living well with vitiligo, and if it’s getting you down I can help with that too. You don’t have to carry the stares on your own."

"So: I’ll check your thyroid, refer you to the skin specialists for treatment options, point you to camouflage and a support group, and we’ll keep an eye on your mood. Take that one fact with you for the doubters — it isn’t catching. Come back and see me; I want to know how YOU are doing, not just the patches."

f.learning: Well-demarcated depigmented (milk-white) macules/patches at characteristic sites (hands, periorificial face, friction sites), spreading, in an otherwise-well young person is VITILIGO — autoimmune loss of melanocytes. The dermatological tasks are real: confirm the diagnosis and reassure FIRMLY that it is NOT contagious, NOT dangerous and not anyone’s fault (correcting the contagion myth); screen for associated autoimmune disease, especially THYROID; discuss treatment realistically (topical steroids/calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy and specialist options via dermatology, cosmetic camouflage, sun protection of depigmented skin) with HONEST expectations (variable, slow, no guaranteed cure). But the examinable core — the hidden agenda — is the PSYCHOSOCIAL and identity impact, intensified on darker skin and by cultural stigma: staring, comments, refusal to shake hands, family concern about "what people will say", and devastation of confidence, relationships and self ("I feel like a freak"). Acknowledge what it MEANS to him, validate it as central, equip him and his family to counter the contagion myth and stigma, screen and support mood, and signpost camouflage and peer support — treating the person and the meaning, not just the macules.

knowledge.guideline: British Association of Dermatologists guidelines for the management of people with vitiligo 2021 · NICE NG222
knowledge.summary: Well-demarcated milk-white patches on the hands and around the eyes and mouth in a well young adult is vitiligo. Say clearly it is not contagious, screen thyroid, offer realistic treatment and camouflage, and treat the psychosocial impact as the main problem.

points.t: Acquired, sharply defined, depigmented (milk-white) macules and patches, often symmetrical, favouring the hands, face around the eyes and mouth, and friction sites; new patches can appear at sites of injury. A Wood’s lamp accentuates depigmentation. Differentials include pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation and pityriasis alba.
Vitiligo is an autoimmune loss of pigment cells. It cannot be caught, is not caused by hygiene or diet, and does not harm physical health. Stating this plainly is itself a treatment.

BAD 2021 recommends checking thyroid function and thyroid antibodies to identify people more likely to develop autoimmune thyroid disease. Be alert to other autoimmune conditions if symptoms suggest them.

BAD 2021: a potent or very potent topical corticosteroid for limited non-facial disease; topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily as an alternative, particularly on the face (unlicensed use, dose per BNF). Narrowband UVB phototherapy through dermatology for more extensive or active disease. Response is slow and variable; hands and lips respond poorly.
Skin camouflage matched to the patient’s skin tone is effective and available through specialist camouflage services. Depigmented skin burns easily; high-factor sunscreen on patches.

BAD 2021 highlights the psychological burden of vitiligo, which is often greater where contrast with skin tone is high and where stigma exists. Ask about mood and, where low, assess and support per NICE NG222; signpost peer support.

model.text: Hello Anand, I’m Dr Lee. Tell me what’s been going on.

These white patches keep appearing and spreading — my hands, round my eyes and mouth. People stare, they ask what’s wrong with me, some won’t shake my hand. My family are worried what people will say. I feel like a freak. I want to know what it is, whether it’s catching, and can you make it go away?

That’s a lot to be carrying, and I’m sorry people have reacted like that. I’ll answer all three of your questions. First I’d like to understand the patches and have a look, then talk about how it’s affecting you, and then agree a plan. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges impact and sets an agenda that covers his three questions

model.text: Yes, fine.
When did you first notice them, and how quickly have they spread?
A few months ago, on my hands. Then round my eyes and mouth. They’re getting bigger.
Are they completely white, or paler than your normal skin? Any itch, scale, redness or numbness?
model.why: Depigmentation versus hypopigmentation; excludes fungal, inflammatory and anaesthetic lesions

model.text: Completely white. They don’t itch or feel different.

Could you hold your hands up to the camera? … And your face? … Thank you. These are sharply edged, milk-white patches, on both hands and around your eyes and mouth. I’d like to see you in person to look more closely, but this looks typical of vitiligo.
model.why: Examination adapted to video with face-to-face follow-up

model.text: Any tiredness, weight change, feeling hot or cold, palpitations, or thirst?
model.why: Screens for associated thyroid disease and diabetes

model.text: No, I feel fine in myself.
Does anyone in your family have vitiligo, thyroid problems or other immune conditions?
Not that I know of.
You said you feel like a freak. What has this been like day to day?
I hide my hands. I don’t want to meet people. When someone won’t shake my hand I just want to disappear.
That sounds really painful. How has your mood been — are you still enjoying things, sleeping, seeing friends?
I’m avoiding people. I feel low, but I’m not going to do anything stupid.
Thank you for saying that. And your family — what are they worried about?
What people will say. None of us really know what it is.
What did you think it might be before today?
I didn’t know. I was scared it was catching, or something serious.

Let me answer your first two questions straight away. This is vitiligo. The immune system stops the cells that make skin colour from working in those areas. It is not catching — no one can get it from you, and shaking hands is completely safe. It isn’t dangerous to your health, and nothing you did caused it.
model.why: Confident diagnosis and firm correction of the contagion myth

model.text: So it’s not an infection?
No. It’s common, including in people of South Asian heritage. If it would help, I can give you written information from the skin specialists to show your family.
model.why: Equips him to counter stigma at home

model.text: That would help. They’d believe it from a doctor.
Because vitiligo is linked with thyroid problems, I’d like a blood test for thyroid function and thyroid antibodies.

On making it go away, I’ll be honest rather than over-promise. There are treatments that can bring colour back or stop spread — a strong steroid cream, or a different ointment for the face — and light treatment through the skin specialists. They work slowly and unevenly, and hands respond less well than the face.
model.why: Realistic treatment options and honest expectations

model.text: So it might not come back.

It may partly come back, and treatment can slow it down. There’s also skin camouflage — specialist make-up matched to your skin tone — which many people find really good. And the white skin burns easily, so sunscreen on the patches matters.
Given how fast it’s spreading, how visible it is and how it’s affecting you, I’d like to refer you to dermatology to discuss treatment, including light treatment. Would you like that?
Yes, please.
And the low mood — there are support groups of people with vitiligo, and talking therapy if you’d like it. You don’t need to face the staring on your own.
If your mood gets worse, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day. I’ll see you in person in two weeks with the thyroid result, and we’ll go through the referral.
model.why: Safety-net on mood and booked follow-up

model.text: Okay.
If someone says it’s catching, what will you tell them?
model.why: Teach-back focused on the contagion myth

model.text: That it’s vitiligo, it’s an immune thing, it can’t be caught and it isn’t my fault.
Exactly. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
No. That’s the first time I’ve felt normal about it.

social.t: Visible patches on darker skin, the common belief that it is catching, and worry about what the community will say all add to the burden. Address beliefs respectfully.
Hiding his hands and avoiding people after refused hand-shakes — explore work and relationships and the effect on confidence.

legal.t: A severe disfigurement is treated as having a substantial adverse effect under the Equality Act 2010, so extensive visible vitiligo may count as a disability. This could matter if he faces discrimination at work.

professional.t: Topical tacrolimus for vitiligo is off-label; explain this and record the discussion (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021).
Recognise how skin tone changes the visibility and meaning of vitiligo; avoid assumptions and ask what it means to him (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Vitiligo Support UK for peer support, Changing Faces for skin camouflage and support with visible difference, BAD patient information leaflet, NHS Talking Therapies self-referral.

Symptoms of thyroid disease, diabetes or other autoimmunity
Low mood, withdrawal or thoughts of self-harm
Itch, scale, numbness or inflammation — reconsider the diagnosis
psychosocial: Hides his hands, avoids people; some refuse to shake his hand
Family and cultural worry about what people will say
ice: Concern: stigma, rejection and family reputation

playbook.diagnosis: “This is vitiligo — your immune system has switched off the colour-making cells in those patches. It isn’t catching, isn’t dangerous and isn’t your fault.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your skin has cells that make its colour, like painters. In vitiligo the immune system tells some painters to stop in certain patches. Nothing has got in from outside — so no one can catch it.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked three things: what it is, whether it’s catching, and whether it can go away. It’s vitiligo, it can’t be caught, and treatment can help but I’ll be honest that it’s slow.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the stigma, give him words and written information for his family, and offer camouflage and peer support.
sharedPlan: Dermatology referral for treatment options including phototherapy; topical treatment per BAD 2021
Skin camouflage, sunscreen on patches, peer and psychological support
safetyNet: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — contact the same day
Review in two weeks with results

pitfalls.intro: The dermatology here is simple. The station is failed by treating the skin and missing the person: the contagion myth, the stigma and his low mood.

items.fail: Not saying clearly that vitiligo is not contagious.
items.why: He asked directly, and the contagion myth drives the stigma he faces. An unanswered question is a missed ICE item.
items.fix: “It is not catching — shaking hands is completely safe.” Then give written information.

items.why: BAD 2021 recommends thyroid function and antibodies; omission is incomplete management.
items.fix: Explain the link and arrange the tests.

items.fail: Promising a cure, or saying nothing works.
items.why: Both are inaccurate and damage trust.
items.fix: Describe topical treatment and phototherapy honestly: helpful, slow, variable, hands respond poorly.

items.fail: Moving past “I feel like a freak” to ask about symptoms.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The psychosocial impact is the heart of the station.
items.fix: “You said you feel like a freak — tell me what that’s been like.”

items.why: Cultural beliefs shape how he lives with vitiligo; dismissal alienates.
items.fix: Respect the worry and help him explain it to them.

items.why: He reports low mood and withdrawal; a missing safety-net is unsafe.
items.fix: Name same-day contact for thoughts of self-harm and book review with results.

BAD 2021 highlights the psychological burden of vitiligo, which is often greater where contrast with skin tone is high and where stigma exists. Ask about mood and, where low, assess and support per NICE NG222; signpost peer support.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him list his three questions and acknowledged the staring and refused hand-shakes before narrowing.
Social avoidance, family and cultural worry about “what people will say”, and uncertainty at home about what it is.
Followed “I feel like a freak”, the refused hand-shakes and the family’s worry.
Idea (catching or serious); concern (stigma, identity, family); expectation (a name, is it catching, a cure).
Video look at hands and face with face-to-face offer; thyroid function and thyroid antibodies (BAD 2021).
Vitiligo versus pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation and other causes; screened for associated autoimmunity.
Asked about thyroid and diabetes symptoms, and asked directly about mood and self-harm.
Named vitiligo confidently and stated plainly: not contagious, not dangerous, not his fault.
Realistic treatment (topical steroid or tacrolimus, phototherapy via dermatology), camouflage, sunscreen, dermatology referral by agreement.
Low mood addressed with peer support and talking therapy; written information for his family.
Mood safety-net, thyroid result and referral review in two weeks, teach-back on the contagion myth.

social.t: Visible patches on darker skin, the common belief that it is catching, and worry about what the community will say all add to the burden. Address beliefs respectfully.
Hiding his hands and avoiding people after refused hand-shakes — explore work and relationships and the effect on confidence.

legal.t: A severe disfigurement is treated as having a substantial adverse effect under the Equality Act 2010, so extensive visible vitiligo may count as a disability. This could matter if he faces discrimination at work.

professional.t: Topical tacrolimus for vitiligo is off-label; explain this and record the discussion (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021).
Recognise how skin tone changes the visibility and meaning of vitiligo; avoid assumptions and ask what it means to him (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Vitiligo Support UK for peer support, Changing Faces for skin camouflage and support with visible difference, BAD patient information leaflet, NHS Talking Therapies self-referral.

redFlags: Rapid spread or new patches at injury sites — active disease, earlier specialist input
Symptoms of thyroid disease, diabetes or other autoimmunity
Low mood, withdrawal or thoughts of self-harm
Itch, scale, numbness or inflammation — reconsider the diagnosis
psychosocial: Hides his hands, avoids people; some refuse to shake his hand
Family and cultural worry about what people will say
ice: Concern: stigma, rejection and family reputation
Expectation: a name, whether it’s catching, and a cure

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is vitiligo — your immune system has switched off the colour-making cells in those patches. It isn’t catching, isn’t dangerous and isn’t your fault.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your skin has cells that make its colour, like painters. In vitiligo the immune system tells some painters to stop in certain patches. Nothing has got in from outside — so no one can catch it.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked three things: what it is, whether it’s catching, and whether it can go away. It’s vitiligo, it can’t be caught, and treatment can help but I’ll be honest that it’s slow.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the stigma, give him words and written information for his family, and offer camouflage and peer support.
sharedPlan: Dermatology referral for treatment options including phototherapy; topical treatment per BAD 2021
Skin camouflage, sunscreen on patches, peer and psychological support
safetyNet: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm — contact the same day
Review in two weeks with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The dermatology here is simple. The station is failed by treating the skin and missing the person: the contagion myth, the stigma and his low mood.

items.fail: Not saying clearly that vitiligo is not contagious.
items.why: He asked directly, and the contagion myth drives the stigma he faces. An unanswered question is a missed ICE item.
items.fix: “It is not catching — shaking hands is completely safe.” Then give written information.

items.why: BAD 2021 recommends thyroid function and antibodies; omission is incomplete management.
items.fix: Explain the link and arrange the tests.

items.fail: Promising a cure, or saying nothing works.
items.why: Both are inaccurate and damage trust.
items.fix: Describe topical treatment and phototherapy honestly: helpful, slow, variable, hands respond poorly.

items.fail: Moving past “I feel like a freak” to ask about symptoms.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The psychosocial impact is the heart of the station.
items.fix: “You said you feel like a freak — tell me what that’s been like.”

items.why: Cultural beliefs shape how he lives with vitiligo; dismissal alienates.
items.fix: Respect the worry and help him explain it to them.

items.why: He reports low mood and withdrawal; a missing safety-net is unsafe.
items.fix: Name same-day contact for thoughts of self-harm and book review with results.
